title: The Tanya's two souls
hookLine: the Tanya describes an animal soul and a godly soul in each person
carry: two souls, one city: let the godly soul lead

lines: MORE THAN ONE VOICE IN THERE.
cards: The alarm goes off. One voice says: five more minutes, you've earned it. Another says: get up, there's someone you promised to call.
You're hungry and someone at the table is hungrier. One voice says take the bigger piece. Another says pass it.
An argument like that needs more than one voice in there. Yesterday's book, the Tanya, doesn't treat that as a glitch. It opens by giving the voices names.

teach.h: THE ANIMAL SOUL: THE LIFE OF THE BODY.
teach.b: Two souls. The Tanya teaches that each Jew has two souls. First, the animal soul.

It's the life of the body: hunger, tiredness, the instinct to protect yourself and get what you need. Animal here isn't an insult. Teachers of the Tanya explain it as the life a person shares with other living creatures.
Its center is self: me first, mine, more.

teach.h: THE GODLY SOUL: A PART OF GOD ABOVE.
teach.b: Second, the godly soul. The Tanya describes it with a phrase borrowed from the book of Job: a part of God above. Its pull is toward God, toward giving, toward the good beyond itself.
Proverbs gives a picture that fits: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." Third, the city.
In a later chapter the Tanya compares the body to a small city, and the two souls to two kings, each wanting to rule it. Every thought, every word, every act is a piece of ground one of them wins.
That's yesterday's in-between person, seen from the inside: two kings, one city, and a daily choice about who governs. Fourth, the aim.

teach.h: NOT TO KILL, BUT TO LEAD.
teach.b: The goal isn't to kill the animal soul.
It keeps you alive. The hope, in Chabad teaching, is that the godly soul leads, and that over time even the animal soul's energy, its hunger and drive, can be turned toward good.
Remember the lesson on serving through the body: the appetite isn't the enemy. It's the city's other citizen, waiting to be led well.

how: In Chabad study, the opening chapters of the Tanya on the animal soul and the godly soul are taught as a map of inner life, used to understand the struggle in prayer and in daily choices.

o: a soul made of two halves, one from each parent
an animal soul and a godly soul, each pulling its own way
a soul for this life, swapped for a new one in the next

p: the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD

s: in the Tanya, the animal soul is called animal as an insult
it's the life a person shares with every living creature: hunger, rest, self-protection.
the Tanya compares the two souls to two kings fighting over a small city
the body is the city, and each thought, word and act is ground one of them wins.
the goal is to destroy the animal soul
it keeps you alive. the hope is that the godly soul leads, and the animal soul's energy turns toward good.

games.q: the alarm goes off. the animal soul says five more minutes. what does the Tanya hope for?
o: that the animal soul is silenced forever.
that the godly soul leads, and even the body's energy is turned to good.
that you obey whichever voice is louder.
games.why: the aim isn't to kill the animal soul but to have the godly soul govern the city, and lead the other well.

practice: Listen inside for the animal soul, tired, hungry, wanting this to be over, and without arguing, just hear it: there you are.
Then listen for the quieter voice, the one that leans toward someone else, toward the good, toward God if you pray, and hear it too.
Sit with both for a while, two voices in one small city; if you pray, you can ask that the quieter one lead.

wordCard.voice: Two souls. In the Tanya, the animal soul that gives life to the body, and the godly soul, a part of God above, each pulling toward its own. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: soul, life. The Tanya speaks of a nefesh of the animal and a nefesh of God.
